notes: Large TCC liability trial on boiler house foundation settlement; Arup breach on design verification is clearly decided.

enrichment.short_title: Arup liability for boiler house foundation settlement at Philippine power station
key_facts: Foundations G2 and G5 of the Unit 1 boiler house at a coal-fired power station in Sual, Philippines settled by 46mm and 66mm in May 1997, far exceeding contractual tolerances.
Mirant/CEPAS and SCC claimed about US$62.5m loss against Ove Arup entities for negligent design and supervision relating to the boiler house foundations.
Following preliminary issues and a Court of Appeal decision, the remaining liability trial concerned whether Arup breached FIDIC-based design and site works obligations.
Arup contended settlement was caused by blasting, fill or contractor failures; the claimants argued the ground could not support the assumed 3 MPa bearing pressure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court trial on remaining liability issues after preliminary issues and an appeal; quantum reserved.
enrichment.outcome: Claimants succeed on liability; Arup found in breach of the design agreement for failing to verify design assumptions before construction; limitation issue does not arise on these findings.
enrichment.ratio: Under the FIDIC-based design contract, verification of geotechnical design parameters was part of the designer's duty, not merely a site inspection matter; Arup breached that duty by permitting foundations G2 and G5 to proceed on an unverified bearing-pressure assumption, although several subsidiary allegations of negligence in ground investigation supervision and pre-blinding inspection were rejected.
legal_issues: Whether Arup breached contractual and tortious duties in designing and verifying boiler house foundations
Whether verification of geotechnical assumptions was a design obligation or site inspection matter
Cause of excessive settlement of foundations G2 and G5
Whether Arup was negligent in supervising the 1996 ground investigation
Whether a limitation defence arose
linked_authorities: Henderson v Merrett Syndicates Ltd [1995] 2 AC 145
Bolam v Friern Hospital Management Committee [1957] 1 WLR 582
Caparo Industries plc v Dickman [1990] 2 AC 605
Midland Bank Trust Co Ltd v Hett, Stubbs and Kemp [1979] 1 Ch 384
Samuel Payne & Co Ltd v John Setchell Ltd [2002] BLR 489
Bellefield Computer Services Ltd v Turner [2000] BLR 97

confidence.notes: Core liability findings and design-verification ratio are explicit, though the judgment is lengthy and several subsidiary negligence allegations were rejected.

notes: VAT sports exemption appeal; non-profit-making body analysis under Group 10 and Sixth Directive is clearly reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: VAT exemption for sporting services supplied by a wholly owned subsidiary
key_facts: Messenger Leisure Developments Ltd supplied sporting services and sought exemption as a non-profit-making body under Schedule 9 Group 10 VATA 1994.
The company was a wholly owned subsidiary of Leisure Developments Ltd, a profit-making parent whose activities were inextricably linked with the appellant's.
The VAT and Duties Tribunal held the appellant was not a non-profit-making body and assessments totalling substantial VAT were upheld.
The appellant's constitution forbade profit distribution, but the parent could alter its constitution at any time.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal on a point of law from a VAT and Duties Tribunal decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; appellant held not a non-profit-making body eligible for the sporting services VAT exemption.
enrichment.ratio: A body that does not distribute profits to members may still fail to qualify as a non-profit-making organisation if its commercial purpose is indistinguishable from that of a profit-making parent; constitutional bars on distribution and absence of current profit-sharing intention are necessary but not sufficient where the subsidiary has no independent business purpose.
legal_issues: Meaning of non-profit-making body under Schedule 9 Group 10 VATA 1994
Construction of Article 13A(1)(m) of the Sixth VAT Directive
Whether a wholly owned subsidiary of a commercial parent can qualify for the exemption
Application of the ECJ decision in Staatssecretaris van Financiën v Vereniging voor Educatie en Vorming Kennemer (Case C-174/00)
linked_authorities: Staatssecretaris van Financiën v Vereniging voor Educatie en Vorming Kennemer (Case C-174/00) [2002] STC 489

confidence.notes: Tribunal findings, statutory framework and dismissal of the appeal are clearly stated.

notes: Costs-only appeal; prosecution costs order quashed where judge did not consider undischarged bankrupt status and ten-year discharge.

enrichment.short_title: Prosecution costs order quashed for undischarged bankrupt
key_facts: Port was convicted after a long trial of managing a company while an undischarged bankrupt.
He was sentenced to imprisonment and ordered to pay £175,000 towards prosecution costs.
He remained an undischarged bankrupt with substantial creditors including the Inland Revenue.
The sentencing judge did not expressly consider bankruptcy status when making the costs order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against prosecution costs order only, by leave granted long after conviction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; prosecution costs order quashed.
enrichment.ratio: A court should not order prosecution costs against an undischarged bankrupt without expressly considering bankruptcy status and the effect of automatic discharge; an order intended to bite only after ten years is inappropriate without that analysis.
legal_issues: Whether prosecution costs may be ordered against an undischarged bankrupt
Relevance of automatic discharge from a subsequent bankruptcy
Duty to consider defendant's insolvency when making costs orders

confidence.notes: Costs-only appeal with clear ratio on bankruptcy and costs.

notes: Interlocutory restrictive covenant injunction application; balance of convenience and serious issue analysis are detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Tensator interlocutory injunction to enforce former employees' restrictive covenants
key_facts: Tensator Group sought interlocutory relief against four former employees who joined a competing business, Xtracs Ltd, selling queue-management and display products.
The application focused on enforcing non-competition, non-dealing, non-solicitation and confidentiality covenants in disputed employment contracts.
Former employees had given undertakings on confidential information and some inspection relief; the claimants' particulars were served seven weeks late.
The competing business was much smaller than Tensator but operated in an overlapping product area.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application for injunctive relief to enforce post-termination restrictive covenants pending trial.
enrichment.outcome: Injunction refused beyond existing undertakings; no further covenant enforcement ordered at this stage.
enrichment.ratio: On an interlocutory application, where serious issues exist on covenant reasonableness and contract terms but damages may be an adequate remedy and undertakings already protect confidential information, the balance of convenience does not favour shutting down the defendants' new business before trial.
legal_issues: Whether serious issues to be tried exist on the validity and reasonableness of restrictive covenants
Whether damages are an adequate remedy
Balance of convenience on interlocutory injunction
Whether the claimants' clean hands were affected by alleged improper payments by the managing director
Whether late service of particulars amounted to an abuse of process
linked_authorities: Dering v Earl of Winchelsea (1787) 1 Cox Eq Cas 318

confidence.notes: Interlocutory outcome and reasoning are clear, though covenant reasonableness remains unresolved for trial.

notes: Judicial review on prison licence recall after section 47 Mental Health Act transfer; statutory interaction clearly analysed.

enrichment.short_title: Prison licence recall after transfer to hospital under Mental Health Act section 47
key_facts: The claimant was sentenced to three years' imprisonment for robbery and recalled to prison after breaching licence conditions.
Two days before scheduled release on licence, he was transferred from prison to Rampton Hospital under section 47 Mental Health Act 1983.
After an incident in hospital and subsequent discharge by the Mental Health Review Tribunal, he was recalled to prison for alleged licence breach.
He challenged the lawfulness of recall, arguing the prison sentence and licence regime ceased on hospital transfer.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim challenging recall to prison following section 47 transfer and subsequent hospital discharge.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; recall held lawful because the prison sentence and licence powers continued despite hospital transfer.
enrichment.ratio: A section 47 transfer direction does not terminate the underlying prison sentence or extinguish Criminal Justice Act licence and recall powers; the Mental Health Act regime operates alongside, not in place of, the sentence for a transferred short-term prisoner.
legal_issues: Effect of a section 47 transfer on an existing prison sentence
Whether licence conditions and recall powers survive hospital transfer
Interaction between Mental Health Act 1983 and Criminal Justice Act release provisions
Lawfulness of recall following discharge from hospital by the Mental Health Review Tribunal
index_terms: Secretary of State for the Home Department

confidence.notes: Statutory analysis and dismissal of the claim are directly addressed; leave to appeal was contemplated.

notes: Short sentencing appeal; incompatibility of concurrent custody and hospital order is clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Quashing concurrent custody sentences incompatible with hospital order
key_facts: The appellant pleaded guilty to manslaughter and received a section 37 hospital order with an unlimited section 41 restriction order.
On the same occasion he received concurrent sentences of detention in a young offender institution for dangerous driving and excess alcohol offences.
Immediate transfer to hospital was inconsistent in practice with immediate commencement of custodial sentences.
Driving disqualification and extended driving test requirements were not challenged.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence by leave of the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; custodial sentences quashed with no separate penalty for the driving offences, but disqualification and extended driving test orders remain.
enrichment.ratio: Although lawfully open, it is inappropriate in practical terms to impose immediate custodial sentences concurrently with a hospital order requiring immediate transfer to a mental hospital; where both are imposed, the custodial terms should be quashed while ancillary driving orders may stand.
legal_issues: Compatibility of hospital orders with concurrent custodial sentences
Appropriate disposal for motoring offences sentenced alongside manslaughter and a hospital order
Whether driving disqualification should survive quashing of custodial terms

confidence.notes: Short judgment with a clear and unambiguous appellate disposition.

notes: Zimbabwe asylum appeal; IAT error on internal relocation and section 101 jurisdiction is clearly identified.

enrichment.short_title: Zimbabwe asylum appeal: internal relocation and IAT error of law
key_facts: A Zimbabwean national claimed asylum based on persecution by ZANU-PF war veterans and the CIO linked to Ndebele ethnicity and Liberty Party membership.
An adjudicator allowed the appeal, finding no safe internal relocation and that food distribution depended on party membership.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal allowed the Secretary of State's appeal, holding the adjudicator misunderstood evidence on food sales in Beitbridge.
The IAT also misstated the section 101 threshold for appeals on points of law only.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with permission against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal determination.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; IAT decision set aside and the adjudicator's allowance of the asylum appeal restored.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 101 of the 2002 Act the IAT may interfere only where the adjudicator erred in law; here the IAT wrongly substituted its own factual assessment on internal relocation and food availability, and there was no legal error in the adjudicator's persecution findings warranting interference.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator erred in law on internal relocation within Zimbabwe
Proper construction of section 101 Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002
Assessment of risk of persecution for Ndebele and opposition supporters in Zimbabwe
Whether food distribution policies made relocation unduly harsh

confidence.notes: Appellate reasoning on section 101 and the IAT's legal error is explicit, though country conditions evidence is fact-specific.

notes: Robbery sentence appeal against vulnerable victim; manifest excessiveness test applied clearly.

enrichment.short_title: Robbery of vulnerable homosexual victim: sentence appeal refused
key_facts: Toomey and Francis pleaded guilty on re-arraignment to robbery after forcing entry to a vulnerable homosexual man's flat and demanding money.
The offenders had previously bullied the victim for money; Toomey smashed a window with a hammer and both overpowered the complainant.
Toomey was sentenced to eight years and Francis to seven years' imprisonment; false imprisonment and theft counts were left on the file.
Both had previous convictions for violence and Toomey was on licence at the time.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed applications for leave to appeal against sentence after refusal by the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Applications refused; sentences of eight and seven years held not manifestly excessive.
enrichment.ratio: For a single robbery against a vulnerable victim in his own home, preceded by sustained bullying and committed by offenders with violent records, sentences at the upper end of the guideline range are severe but not arguably manifestly excessive even where pleas were late.
legal_issues: Whether eight and seven year sentences were manifestly excessive
Appropriate starting point for robbery against a vulnerable victim
Effect of late guilty pleas and lack of remorse on sentence
Relevance of previous violent convictions and commission while on licence
linked_authorities: Attorney General's Reference No 48 of 2000, R v Johnson [2001] 1 Cr App R (S) 423

confidence.notes: Facts, guideline reference and refusal of leave are clearly stated in a short judgment.

notes: Litigant-in-person boundary dispute permission application; refusal grounds are clearly explained.

enrichment.short_title: Boundary and adverse possession dispute: permission to appeal refused
key_facts: Neighbours at Hughes Close, Worcestershire disputed the boundary between 37 Hughes Close and 29a Hughes Close.
A recorder declared the boundary along a line on an expert plan and awarded £410 damages plus costs to the claimants.
Mr Cottrill, acting in person, sought permission to appeal out of time, alleging unfair treatment and new evidence.
The judge had found the claimants adversely possessed a fenced strip and rejected the defendant's gardening and weedkiller evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal, extension of time, stay of execution and admission of new evidence following a county court boundary trial.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal, extension of time and stay all refused.
enrichment.ratio: Allegations of judicial unfairness or case-management complaints do not ground an appeal without identifying a specific legal or evidential error affecting the boundary or adverse possession findings; knowledge that a fence was misplaced does not defeat a claim based on exclusive possession.
legal_issues: Whether the recorder erred in fixing the boundary line
Whether adverse possession of the fenced strip was established
Whether the judge's conduct deprived the defendant of a fair hearing
Whether new evidence should be admitted on appeal

confidence.notes: Procedural outcome and reasons for refusing permission are clearly articulated by Lady Justice Arden.

notes: Employment tribunal strike-out appeal; unfair hearing on non-attendance is clearly established.

enrichment.short_title: Employment tribunal strike-out set aside for unfair non-attendance hearing
key_facts: Mrs Obasa brought employment tribunal claims of unfair dismissal and race, sex and disability discrimination against London Borough of Islington.
After a protracted history, the tribunal struck out the remaining discrimination claims for want of prosecution when she failed to attend the merits hearing.
She had applied to return under a maternity and parenthood scheme and the council disputed continuing employment after June 1995.
The Court of Appeal held she did not receive a fair hearing on whether her non-attendance was intentional and contumelious.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with extension of time against an Employment Appeal Tribunal decision affirming strike-out for want of prosecution.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; employment tribunal strike-out order set aside and matter remitted for directions before a merits hearing.
enrichment.ratio: Where a litigant offers explanations for non-attendance at an employment tribunal hearing, including illness abroad, strike-out under the want-of-prosecution rule requires a fair oral hearing before those explanations are rejected; failure to afford that hearing renders the strike-out unjust.
legal_issues: Whether strike-out for want of prosecution was properly made
Whether the claimant's non-attendance was intentional and contumelious
Fairness of proceeding in the claimant's absence without hearing her explanations
Application of Birkett v James principles in employment tribunal procedure

confidence.notes: Appellate reasoning on procedural fairness and the remittal order are clearly expressed.
